title: Building an RJ Nexus Theme: A Widget-First Approach, Using Spotlight as the Example
headings: Building an RJ Nexus Theme: A Widget-First Approach, Using Spotlight as the Example | Table of Contents | 1. Why widget-first? | 2. Folder structure | 3. `theme.json`: the theme's passport | 4. The ServiceProvider: your theme's entry point | 5. Your first widget, step by step | 5.1. The PHP class | 5.2. The Blade view | 5.3. Three technical lessons from the real project | 6. `BaseWidget` helpers | 7. The Customizer and `layout.blade.php` | 8. Custom page templates | 9. The hook system | 10. The starter content mechanism | 11. Publishing your theme | Pre-release checklist | Registration: `rj-registration` | 12. Best practices and traps from the real project | Do | Watch out for | Summary
content: Building an RJ Nexus Theme: A Widget-First Approach, Using Spotlight as the Example A hands-on tutorial for developers A classic CMS theme is usually hundreds of PHP templates plus a pile of CSS and JS. RJ Nexus works differently: a theme is a collection of widgets for building a site. The main design of each page comes from the Builder in the admin panel. The theme only handles special cases: layout, home, archive, single-page and single-post. In this guide we'll use the Spotlight theme as a reference and walk through building a working theme from scratch. Table of Contents Why widget-first? Folder structure theme.json: the theme's passport The ServiceProvider: your theme's entry point Your first widget, step by step BaseWidget helpers The Customizer and layout.blade.php Custom page templates The hook system The starter content mechanism Publishing your theme Best practices and traps from the real project --- 1. Why widget-first? Lightweight. Only the widgets used on a page are rendered. The CSS and JS of the 20 unused widgets never load. Isolated. Each widget scopes its own and with a unique #uid, so widgets can't break each other's styles. Reusable. The same widget works on any page, in the header, in the footer and in popups. A theme ends up being three things: widgets, layout templates and Customizer settings. 2. Folder structure rj-content/themes/spotlight/ ├── theme.json # theme manifest ├── screenshot.png # theme preview image ├── README.md / CHANGELOG.md / LICENSE ├── assets/ # static files ├── demo/ # data for starter content ├── src/ │ ├── SpotlightServiceProvider.php │ ├── Services/SpotlightStarterContent.php │ └── Widgets/ # one PHP class per widget └── views/ ├── layout.blade.php ├── home.blade.php ├── archive.blade.php ├── single-page.blade.php ├── single-post.blade.php ├── errors/404.blade.php ├── partials/ # loop-card, popup ├── templates/ # contact, landing, full-width └── widgets/ # widget Blade files The rule of thumb: logic lives in src/, markup lives in views/. 3. theme.json: the theme's passport { "name": "Spotlight", "slug": "spotlight", "version": "1.1.4", "namespace": "Spotlight", "provider": "Spotlight\\SpotlightServiceProvider", "requires": { "rj_cms": ">=1.8.6", "php": ">=8.2" }, "views": { "layout": "views/layout.blade.php", "single_post": "views/single-post.blade.php", "single_page": "views/single-page.blade.php", "archive": "views/archive.blade.php" } } Key fields: namespace + provider: this is how the CMS knows which class to boot. requires: blocks installation on an incompatible CMS or PHP version. views: templates for the special page types. custom_templates: templates an editor can pick when creating a page (contact, landing, full-width). customizer: settings for colors, fonts, layout and so on. Each control has a type, a label and a default. assets.css and assets.js can stay empty, since widgets ship their own styles inline. If you do need a global file, layout.blade.php picks it up automatically through $activeTheme->metadata()['assets']. 4. The ServiceProvider: your theme's entry point Where WordPress has functions.php, RJ Nexus has a Laravel ServiceProvider: namespace Spotlight; use Illuminate\Support\ServiceProvider; use Spotlight\Widgets\SpotlightVideoShowcaseWidget; class SpotlightServiceProvider extends ServiceProvider { public function boot(): void { // Tell Laravel where the spotlight:: view namespace lives $this->loadViewsFrom(DIR . '/../views', 'spotlight'); $this->registerWidgets(); $this->maybeSetupStarterContent(); } protected function registerWidgets(): void { if (!functionexists('rjadd_filter')) return; rjaddfilter('builder.widgets', function ($existing) { return array_merge($existing, [ new SpotlightVideoShowcaseWidget(), // more widgets... ]); }); } } Two things matter here: loadViewsFrom(..., 'spotlight') is what makes view('spotlight::widgets.video-showcase') work. Widgets aren't registered directly. They're appended to the list through the builder.widgets filter, which keeps the theme and the Builder loosely coupled. 5. Your first widget, step by step Every widget extends BaseWidget. It gives you defaults(), the shared style fields (bgtype, boxshadow, and so on), animation fields and a set of helper methods. 5.1. The PHP class namespace Spotlight\Widgets; use App\Widgets\BaseWidget; class SpotlightVideoShowcaseWidget extends BaseWidget { public function id(): string { return 'spotlight-video-showcase'; } public function name(): string { return __('Spotlight Video Showcase'); } public function category(): string { return 'spotlight'; } public function description(): string { return __('Display a video inside a sleek browser mockup with a lightbox play button.'); } public function contexts(): array { return ['page', 'block']; } public function schema(): array { return [ ['name' => 'title', 'type' => 'text', 'label' => __('Title'), 'default' => __('See it in action'), 'tab' => 'content'], ['name' => 'videourl', 'type' => 'text', 'label' => _('Video URL (YouTube, Vimeo, or MP4)'), 'default' => '', 'tab' => 'content'], ['name' => 'coverimage', 'type' => 'image', 'label' => _('Cover Image'), 'default' => '', 'tab' => 'content'], ]; } public function render(array $settings): string { $uid = 'vs_' . substr(md5(uniqid('', true)), 0, 8); return view('spotlight::widgets.video-showcase', compact('settings', 'uid'))->render(); } } What each method does: | Method | Purpose | |---|---| | id() | Unique identifier. Builder blocks are stored with it | | category() | Grouping in the widget panel | | contexts() | Where the widget can be used (page, block) | | schema() | The fields shown in the admin panel | | render() | Returns the final HTML | Field types seen in BaseWidget and the Spotlight widgets: text, textarea, image, color, select, number, media. Tab values: content, style, advanced. 5.2. The Blade view The core rules of views/widgets/video-showcase.blade.php: @php $uid = $uid ?? ('vs_' . substr(md5(uniqid('', true)), 0, 8)); $title = $settings['title'] ?? ''; $videoUrl = $settings['video_url'] ?? ''; @endphp ... #{{ $uid }}.rj-vs { / every rule starts with the uid / } (function () { var root = document.getElementById(@js($uid)); if (!root) return; // logic for this widget only })(); Four rules to follow: Every CSS rule starts with #uid. A second instance of the widget on the same page keeps working. JS lives inside an IIFE. No globals leak out. Use $settings['key'] ?? ''. The editor may not have filled in a field yet, or the field may have been added after the block was saved. {{ }} escapes automatically. When passing a value into JS, use @js(...). 5.3. Three technical lessons from the real project Move the lightbox to . A position: fixed element doesn't cover the viewport when it sits inside a transformed ancestor. The fix: document.body.appendChild(lightbox); Pause infinite animations when off-screen. new IntersectionObserver(function (e) { root.classList.toggle('rj-idle', !e[0].isIntersecting); }, { threshold: 0.08 }).observe(root); #uid.rj-idle , #uid.rj-idle ::before { animation-play-state: paused !important; } Validate the video URL. To block schemes like javascript:, only allow addresses starting with http(s):// or /. Build the embed URL with a regex for YouTube and Vimeo, and use a element for .mp4/.webm/.ogg. Support prefers-reduced-motion too, with animation: none. 6. BaseWidget helpers Don't rewrite the same code every time: | Helper | What it does | |---|---| | defaults() / fullDefaults() | Collects default values from the schema | | commonStyleSchema() | Background, shadow, align_self, order fields | | advancedSchema() | Animation, hover, CSS ID/class | | applyAnimation($html, $settings) | Wraps the HTML in an rj-animate-* class | | backgroundCss($settings) | Returns CSS for classic and gradient backgrounds | | boxShadowCss($shadow) | Maps sm/md/lg/xl to CSS | | linkAttrs($settings, 'link') | href, target, rel="noopener nofollow" | | iconSvg('arrow-right', 20) | Built-in SVG icon set | | repeaterItems($settings, 'items') | Safely turns repeater fields into an array | | escape() / attr() | htmlspecialchars and an attribute builder | | dimensionCss() / spacingStyle() | Turns padding/margin values into CSS | If you build HTML in PHP instead of Blade, run every user-supplied value through escape(). 7. The Customizer and layout.blade.php Theme settings are declared in theme.json and read in templates like this: $cPrimary = rjthememod('primary_color', null, 'colors'); Three parameters: key, default, section name. The main principle: never write a user-controlled value straight into CSS. Validate it first. Spotlight does it like this: $sanitizeColor = function ($value, $default) { $value = is_string($value) ? trim($value) : ''; return preg_match('/^#[0-9a-fA-F]{3,8}$/', $value) ? $value : $default; }; $allowedFonts = ['Inter', 'Figtree', 'Roboto', 'Open Sans', 'Lato', 'Poppins', 'system-ui']; if (!in_array($fontBody, $allowedFonts, true)) $fontBody = 'Inter'; $fontSizeBase = max(12, min(24, (int) rjthememod('fontsizebase', 16, 'typography'))); The validated values then become CSS variables: :root { --rj-primary: {{ $cPrimary }}; --rj-bg: {{ $cBg }}; --rj-container: {{ $containerWidth }}px; } If your widgets use var(--rj-primary), they all follow along when someone changes the color in the Customizer. 8. Custom page templates single-page.blade.php is simple at its core: @extends('theme::layout') @section('content') @if($header) {!! rjrendertemplate($header) !!} @endif @if($page) @if($page->isBuilderMode() && $page->hasBlocks()) {!! rjrenderblocks($page->blocks['blocks'] ?? []) !!} @elseif(!empty($page->content)) {!! $page->content !!} @endif @endif @if($footer) {!! rjrendertemplate($footer) !!} @endif @endsection Three helpers do the work: rjrenderblocks($blocks) turns Builder blocks into HTML. Each block is looked up in WidgetRegistry, dynamic values are resolved (rjresolvedynamics), then render() is called. rjrendertemplate($template) renders header and footer templates. rjthememod() reads a Customizer value. There's no wrapper in this template, so the Builder's design shows up exactly as built. The theme only adds shared "atmosphere" layers such as the background video and the starfield. archive and single-post are different. There the theme designs the page itself (sidebar, categories, comments), because those parts aren't built with the Builder. 9. The hook system rjaddfilter and rjaddaction follow WordPress logic: // Filter: modifies a value and returns it rjaddfilter('builder.widgets', function ($widgets) { $widgets[] = new MyWidget(); return $widgets; }, 10, 1); // Action: does something, returns nothing rjaddaction('some.event', function ($arg1, $arg2) { // ... }, 10, 2); Priority: lower numbers run first (default 10). acceptedArgs: how many arguments are passed to the callback. Safety: if a callback throws, HookRegistry catches it and logs it, and the site keeps running. For filters, the value stays unchanged. Use rjremovefilter to remove a callback and rjhasfilter to check for one. Two limitations are worth knowing about. didAction() currently never increments its counter, and there's no theme activation hook. Both are worth adding to the CMS core. 10. The starter content mechanism So that a freshly activated theme doesn't leave the site looking empty, demo content (pages, menus, posts) can be created automatically. Spotlight does it like this: protected function maybeSetupStarterContent(): void { if (!functionexists('rjgetoption') || !functionexists('rjsetoption')) return; try { $activeTheme = rjgetoption('active_theme', ''); if ($activeTheme === 'spotlight' && !rjgetoption('spotlightstartercontent_imported')) { SpotlightStarterContent::run(); rjsetoption('spotlightstartercontent_imported', true); } } catch (\Throwable $e) { logger()->error('Spotlight Starter Content Error: ' . $e->getMessage()); } } The logic: If the active theme is spotlight and the spotlightstartercontent_imported flag is missing, run() executes. After a successful run the flag is set to true, so it never runs again. If you switch to another theme, nothing is imported. If you switch back, the flag is still set, so it doesn't import a second time either. Things to watch: Make it idempotent. If run() throws halfway, the flag isn't set and it retries on every request. Inside run(), check things like "does a page with this slug already exist?" Don't do heavy work inside a request. The first visitor shouldn't have to wait. Ideally this runs from an activation hook or a queue. To re-import, delete the spotlightstartercontent_imported option. Keep demo images and data in the demo/ folder, not in code. 11. Publishing your theme Pre-release checklist [ ] version, requires, author and repo in theme.json are correct. [ ] screenshot.png (plus screenshot-1.png and screenshot-2.png for the gallery) is in the repo. [ ] README.md, CHANGELOG.md and LICENSE exist. [ ] A GitHub Release is created with the ZIP attached. Registration: rj-registration Themes are added to themes.json in the rj-nexus/rj-registration repo through a pull request: { "repo": "rj-nexus/spotlight", "name": "Spotlight", "author": "rj-nexus", "version": "1.1.4", "verified": true, "category": "general", "tags": ["dark", "glassmorphism", "ai", "saas", "premium"], "logo": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rj-nexus/spotlight/main/screenshot.png", "details": { "description": "A dark, modern, builder-first theme...", "features": ["20+ custom premium widgets", "Auto-import starter content on activation"] }, "installation": { "steps": [ "Download the ZIP from the releases page", "Go to Admin → Appearance → Themes", "Upload the ZIP file", "Click Activate" ] }, "development": { "requires": "RJ Nexus >= 1.8.6" } } > Note: the version in theme.json (1.1.4) should match the one in themes.json. Update both on every release. For users, installation is: Admin → Appearance → Themes → upload ZIP → Activate. 12. Best practices and traps from the real project Do Scope all widget CSS with #uid. Always validate user-supplied values (colors, fonts, URLs). Support prefers-reduced-motion and :focus-visible. Control heavy animations with IntersectionObserver. Watch out for Schema and view must match. The video widget's view reads badgetext, playlabel and accent_color, but schema() doesn't define them, so editors can't fill them in. Every key your view reads should exist in the schema. Validate colors inside widgets too. --ac: {{ $accent }} is escaped, but its format isn't checked. Apply the same sanitizeColor logic from the layout. Don't mix up Customizer sections. single-post.blade.php reads backgroundvideo from the bloglist section, while theme.json defines a separate control under blog_single. If the sharing is intentional, document it. If not, fix it. Don't send API keys in URLs. For widgets that use internal AI services (for example Gemini's ?key=), the key can end up in logs. Send it in a header (x-goog-api-key) instead. Don't forget provider registration. If you write a new widget class but don't add it to the builder.widgets list, the Builder will never see it. Clean up duplicated code. In layout.blade.php, $themeAssets is assigned twice. Harmless, but worth tidying. --- Summary Put simply, Spotlight's architecture is that the theme doesn't draw the design itself. It hands you the tools to draw it. That keeps the site light, lets you test each widget on its own, and limits template work to the places that need it: layout, archive and single. Write a widget, register it in builder.widgets, hook your colors into the Customizer, prepare starter content, and send a PR to rj-registration.

content: Languages & Translation RJ Nexus allows you to manage multiple languages, change the admin and frontend locales, translate your content, and fully customize the translation strings. This guide covers everything from adding a new language to using the built-in translation editor. --- 1. Accessing Language Settings Step 1 — From the admin sidebar, navigate to Settings. Step 2 — In the settings grid, locate and click on the Language card. Step 3 — This opens the main Language management screen. --- 2. General Language Settings At the bottom of the Language screen, you will find the core configuration options. Admin Language: Sets the default language for your admin panel. Frontend Language: Sets the default fallback language for your public site. Auto-detect browser language: If enabled, the system automatically sets the locale based on the visitor's browser language. Enable RTL support: Automatically applies Right-to-Left layout direction for languages like Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, and Urdu. --- 3. Managing Languages Add a New Language You can add a new language to the system by clicking the Add Language button. Select Frontend Languages Choose which languages are visible to your visitors on the frontend. Only the selected languages will appear in the frontend language switcher. Edit Language Name You can rename the languages to fit your site's needs. Change Language Flag You can change the country flag associated with a language by uploading a new icon. Delete a Language System languages can be deleted using the trash icon next to the language. --- 4. Using the Translation Editor To translate the static strings (UI text) of your site, click the Translate button next to any language. AI Translation Setup At the bottom of the language settings, you will find the AI Translation option. Important: The Auto Translate feature requires an OpenRouter API key to function. If you haven't set it up yet, follow the AI Setup (OpenRouter) guide. The Translation Screen When you open the translation editor, you will see a detailed interface. Here is a breakdown of the 5 colored areas: Green Box (Auto Translate): Click this to automatically translate missing strings using AI. (Requires OpenRouter setup). Red Box (Search): Use this search bar to find specific keys or translations. You can search in any language to quickly locate and edit a string. Purple Box (Keys): These are the original strings or keys that need to be translated (usually in English). Yellow Box (Strings): This is where the actual translation goes. Edit the text here to change what the user sees. Blue Button (Save): Click this button to save all your changes to the translation files.

headings: Widget Development | Anatomy of a widget | A complete example | The schema | Field types used by built-in widgets | Helpers from `BaseWidget` | Two ways to render | Security rules | Good habits
content: Widget Development Widgets are the building blocks of RJ Builder. A widget is a PHP class that describes its settings and renders its HTML. Themes and plugins are built from widgets too, which keeps pages light and easy to manage block by block. This guide covers the structure of a widget, based on the built-in widgets. Anatomy of a widget A built-in widget lives in app/Widgets/Builtin/, uses the App\Widgets\Builtin namespace and extends App\Widgets\BaseWidget. Every widget implements seven methods: | Method | Returns | Purpose | |---|---|---| | id() | string | A unique identifier, for example text or chinese-festivals. | | name() | string | The name shown in the builder. Wrap it in __() so it can be translated. | | icon() | string | An inline SVG shown next to the name. | | category() | string | The group in the widget panel, for example basic, header or content. | | description() | string | A short description. | | schema() | array | The list of settings fields. | | render(array $settings) | string | The final HTML. | A complete example '; } public function category(): string { return 'content'; } public function description(): string { return __('A highlighted message box.'); } public function schema(): array { return [ [ 'name' => 'message', 'type' => 'textarea', 'label' => __('Message'), 'default' => __('Important information.'), 'tab' => 'content', ], [ 'name' => 'tone', 'type' => 'select', 'label' => __('Tone'), 'default' => 'info', 'tab' => 'style', 'options' => ['info' => ('Info'), 'warning' => ('Warning')], ], [ 'name' => 'color', 'type' => 'color', 'label' => __('Background'), 'default' => '#eff6ff', 'tab' => 'style', ], ]; } public function render(array $settings): string { $message = trim((string) ($settings['message'] ?? '')); if ($message === '') { return ''; } $tone = in_array($settings['tone'] ?? '', ['info', 'warning'], true) ? $settings['tone'] : 'info'; $color = $this->hex($settings['color'] ?? null, '#eff6ff'); $html = ' ' . nl2br($this->escape($message)) . ' '; return $this->applyAnimation($html, $settings); } private function hex(mixed $value, string $default): string { $value = trim((string) $value); return preg_match('/^#(?:[0-9a-f]{3,4}|[0-9a-f]{6}|[0-9a-f]{8})$/i', $value) ? $value : $default; } } > [!IMPORTANT] A widget must be added to the widget list, otherwise it does not appear in the builder. This was the reason three built-in widgets were missing in an earlier release. The schema schema() returns an array of fields. Each field is an array. | Key | Description | |---|---| | name | The key under which the value arrives in $settings. | | type | The field type (see below). | | label | The label in the editor. | | default | The starting value. | | tab | Where the field appears: content or style. | | placeholder | Optional hint text. | | help | Optional help text under the field. | | options | For select: a value => label array. | | min, max, step | For range. | Field types used by built-in widgets | Type | Value you receive | |---|---| | text | A string. | | textarea | A string with line breaks. | | select | One of the option keys, as a string. | | color | A color string such as #2563eb. | | toggle | A boolean (it can arrive as a string, so normalize it). | | range | A number. | | media | A string URL, or an array with a key such as url, src or path. | | dimensions | An array with top, right, bottom, left, unit and linked. | Helpers from BaseWidget Built-in widgets call these helpers on $this: | Helper | Use | |---|---| | escape($value) | Escapes a value for safe HTML output. | | dimensionCss($settings, 'name') | Turns a dimensions field into a CSS value. | | backgroundCss($settings) | Builds background CSS from the common background settings. | | boxShadowCss($settings['box_shadow'] ?? null) | Builds box-shadow CSS. | | cssId($settings) and cssClass($settings) | Return the custom ID and class entered by the user. | | attr(array $attrs) | Builds an HTML attribute string. | | applyAnimation($html, $settings) | Wraps the HTML with the widget's motion settings. | Two ways to render Return HTML from PHP. Good for small widgets. The Text widget builds a tag and returns it. Render a Blade view. Good for larger widgets. Put the view in resources/views/rjbuilder/widgets/builtin/ and return it from render(): return view('rjbuilder.widgets.builtin.logo', [ 'o' => $opts, 'uid' => $uid, ])->render(); Create a unique ID for each instance, so the same widget can appear several times on a page without its CSS or JavaScript clashing: $uid = 'logo_' . substr(md5(uniqid('', true)), 0, 8); In the view, scope all CSS to #{{ $uid }}. Security rules Settings come from the editor, so never trust them. Built-in widgets follow these rules: Allow-list choices. If a value must be one of a few options, check it with in_array() and fall back to a default. Validate colors. Accept only a hex pattern before putting a color into CSS. Clean text. Use strip_tags() and a length limit for titles, or escape() for output. Check URLs. Allow only http, https, mailto, tel, anchors and relative links. Escape in Blade. Use {{ }}, not {!! !!}, for user values. Safe JSON in pages. When you pass data to JavaScript, encode it with JSONHEXTAG, JSONHEXAMP, JSONHEXAPOS and JSONHEXQUOT. Good habits Translate every visible string with __(). Cache heavy calculations with Cache::remember(), and include the interface language in the cache key if the result contains translated text. Return an empty string when there is nothing to show. Show a clear message instead of failing when a dependency is missing. Respect reduced motion in CSS animations: @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce).
